issues.legal_issue: A court reviewing a refusal to approve a professional college should remit the matter for reconsideration rather than directly order that approval be granted.
material_facts: The college had received permission to admit a smaller intake than it sought.
The High Court ordered approval for the larger intake despite the inspection report and the Central Government’s decision limiting admissions.
The governing statutory framework assigned approval of a new dental college to the Central Government, on the Dental Council’s recommendations.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should not have issued a mandamus directly granting approval. If it considered the refusal unlawful or arbitrary, it should have remitted the matter for reinspection and reconsideration by the appropriate authorities.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 10-A of the Dentists Act, 1948, the Central Government grants approval for establishing a dental college, with the Dental Council performing its statutory role. The regulations made under Sections 10-A and 20 prescribe requirements and annual targets for permission and renewal. Where a refusal is unlawful or arbitrary, the appropriate course is reconsideration by the statutory authorities, not a judicial direction granting approval: Medical Council of India v. State of Himachal Pradesh (2000) 5 SCC 63; Union of India v. Era Educational Trust (2000) 5 SCC 57. Regulations within the statutory purpose have mandatory force: Medical Council of India v. State of Karnataka (1998) 6 SCC 131.

predicates.judicial_review_of_refused_college_appro: A court is reviewing a decision refusing approval sought by a professional college.
predicates.refusal_found_unlawful_or_arbitrary: The court finds that the refusal does not comply with the governing law or is arbitrary.

issues.definition: When a court reviewing a refused college approval finds the refusal unlawful or arbitrary, it sends the matter back to the statutory authorities rather than granting approval itself.

issues.legal_issue: Judicial review of decisions by expert educational bodies remains available but is limited, and courts should ordinarily defer to those bodies’ assessment of educational standards and capacity.
material_facts: The Dental Council was the expert body responsible for assessing the college’s infrastructure, staffing and capacity.
The Council’s assessment limited the college’s student intake, while the college challenged that assessment.
The Court considered both the need to respect expert assessment and the possibility that an expert body might act arbitrarily.
issues.conclusion: Courts should not ordinarily take over the functions of expert educational bodies, but they may correct arbitrary action by those bodies.
issues.legal_principle: Judicial review is not excluded where an expert body acts arbitrarily, but courts should be slow to interfere with expert academic assessments. The Court relied on State of Punjab v. Renuka Singla (1994) 1 SCC 175; Krishna Priya Ganguly v. University of Lucknow (1984) 1 SCC 307; State of Maharashtra v. Vikas Sahebrao Roundale (1992) 4 SCC 435; Guru Nanak Dev University v. Parminder Kr. Bansal (1993) 4 SCC 401; and A.P. Christians Medical Educational Society v. Government of A.P. (1986) 2 SCC 667.

predicates.judicial_review_of_expert_educational_de: A court is reviewing an expert body’s decision concerning an educational institution.
predicates.expert_body_has_assessment_role: The body making the decision has responsibility for assessing educational standards, facilities or institutional capacity.

issues.definition: When a court reviews an educational decision made by an expert body, it respects the body’s assessment but may intervene if the decision is unlawful or arbitrary.

issues.legal_issue: Admissions made in reliance on operative court orders in the particular circumstances of the case need not be disturbed, but students may take examinations only if they satisfy the applicable attendance requirements.
material_facts: The college admitted students beyond the intake permitted by the Dental Council.
The High Court had ordered approval for the larger intake, and that order had not been stayed.
Further High Court orders had been made concerning the students and the college.
The students had completed different amounts of study, and the Dental Council’s regulations required minimum attendance before examinations.
issues.conclusion: The admissions were not disturbed in the peculiar circumstances of the case. The students could sit examinations only in accordance with the Dental Council’s attendance requirements.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the operative, unstayed court orders and the particular circumstances as reasons not to disturb the existing admissions, while preserving the requirement that students satisfy the applicable attendance rules. The Court expressly confined its order to the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case.

predicates.appeal_concerning_existing_professional_: The proceeding concerns existing admissions to a professional course challenged in an appeal.
predicates.admissions_relied_on_unstayed_court_orde: The institution made the admissions in reliance on a court order that had not been stayed.
predicates.applicable_attendance_requirements_not_y: The students’ right to take examinations remains subject to attendance requirements that apply to the course.

issues.definition: In an appeal about existing professional-course admissions made in reliance on an unstayed court order, the admissions may remain in place while examination access remains conditional on the applicable attendance requirements.

issues.legal_issue: Current permission and renewals for a professional college may be directed in accordance with the assessed facilities and prescribed conditions when the parties agree to that relief.
material_facts: During the proceedings, the parties agreed that the college’s current facilities justified permission for the proposed intake and renewals for later years of the course.
The college undertook to provide the complete teaching staff required by the regulations, to the satisfaction of the Council and the Central Government.
The parties agreed that the Council would make recommendations and that the Central Government would act on those recommendations.
The Court stated that its order was based on the peculiar facts and circumstances and would not be treated as a precedent.
issues.conclusion: The Court accepted the agreed directions: the Council was to make recommendations consistent with the assessed facilities and the Central Government was to grant appropriate permission and renewals based on those recommendations and the prescribed conditions. The order was not to be treated as a precedent.
issues.legal_principle: The permission and renewal process is governed by Section 10-A of the Dentists Act, 1948, and the regulations made under Sections 10-A and 20. In this case the Court gave effect to the parties’ agreement concerning the facilities, staffing undertaking, Council recommendations and governmental permissions, while expressly limiting the order to the case’s peculiar circumstances.

predicates.dispute_over_professional_college_permis: The proceeding concerns permission or renewal for a professional college.
predicates.parties_agreed_to_relief: The parties agreed on the directions governing permission or renewal.
predicates.current_facilities_support_assessed_inta: The facilities currently available support the student intake assessed in the proceeding.
predicates.college_undertook_required_staffing: The college undertook to provide the required teaching staff to the satisfaction of the relevant authorities.

issues.definition: Where the parties agree on relief in a permission or renewal dispute and the current facilities support the assessed intake, permission and renewals follow the authorities’ recommendations and prescribed conditions.

issues.legal_issue: Students admitted to a professional course may attend classes and take examinations only if they meet the applicable admission eligibility criteria and the required attendance conditions.
material_facts: The Court’s agreed directions permitted eligible students to attend classes and take examinations if they had attended the required number of classes.
One eligibility route required participation in a state common entrance test and the prescribed minimum performance in English and Science in the qualifying examination or entrance test.

A second route applied to other students who met the prescribed minimum performance in English and Science in the qualifying examination, subject to a limit on the number admitted through that route in each batch.
issues.conclusion: Only students satisfying one of the specified eligibility routes could attend classes and take examinations, and examination access also depended on satisfying the required attendance conditions.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the eligibility conditions contained in the parties’ agreed directions and required compliance with the Dental Council’s attendance regulations. These directions were made in the peculiar circumstances of the case and were expressly not to be treated as a precedent.

predicates.professional_course_student_eligibility_: The proceeding concerns whether students admitted to a professional course may attend classes or take examinations.
predicates.state_entrance_route_and_subject_score_t: The student took a state common entrance test and met the prescribed minimum performance in English and Science in the qualifying examination or entrance test.
predicates.other_route_subject_score_threshold_and_: The student who did not qualify through the state entrance route met the prescribed minimum performance in English and Science in the qualifying examination, and admissions through that route stayed within the batch limit.
predicates.required_attendance_completed: The student attended the number of classes required for the relevant examination.

issues.definition: A professional-course student may attend classes and take examinations if the student meets either specified eligibility route, the applicable batch limit is observed for the alternative route, and the student completes the required attendance.
